title: Humidity-induced dynamic coordination drives the oscillatory migration of ions for sustainable energy harvesting

paper_content.abstract: Moisture-induced ion diffusion in nanostructured materials is a promising route for high-performance power generation, yet achieving the continuous ion migration necessary for long-term operation remains challenging. Here, we report a moisture-electricity conversion mechanism capable of sustained electrical output. We demonstrate that humidity fluctuations regulate the dynamic coordination between iodide ions (I-) and iodine molecules (I2), driving the oscillatory migration of I- to generate a continuous alternating ion current (AC). Crucially, this coordination process avoids charge exchange, while electricity generation is achieved through moisture-driven ion transport. The device achieves a current output of 33.2 µA cm-² and exhibits sustainable performance recovery under natural humidity fluctuations. This mechanism remains effective even under minimal humidity gradients (13% RH), ensuring adaptability to diverse weather conditions. Our strategy, applicable to various gel materials, utilizes environmental humidity fluctuations as a power source for ion diffusion, offering a fundamental solution for long-term, autonomous energy harvesting.
paper_content.introduction:
The ubiquitous presence of water in the environment provides a natural reservoir for green energy1. Generating electricity through the electric coupling between functional materials and various forms of water—such as flow, waves, droplets, moisture and evaporation—a new type of energy conversion effect has emerged, which is defined as hydrovoltaic technology2–4. Compared with conventional photovoltaic and wind power technologies, which rely on intermittent and variable sources such as sunlight and wind under specific environmental conditions, hydrovoltaic technology demonstrates significant potential due to the ubiquity of water resources in nature5. Among hydrovoltaic technologies, moisture- and evaporation-driven generators have attracted increasing attention for their virtues of ubiquity, spontaneity, and direct current output6. Evaporation-based power generation represents a passive means of energy harvesting that leverages natural processes instead of mechanical motion7. However, its long-term performance is constrained by the reliance on continuous access to liquid water and is susceptible to climatic fluctuations8. Moisture-electric generators (MEGs) are destined to exploiting omnipresent power sources due to the abundance, accessibility, and all-weather availability of moisture in the ambient environment9–12.

Nevertheless, most existing MEGs operate in a unidirectional migration process of water and ions13–15. When the water and ions migration tend to equilibrate, the MEGs will stop outputting electrical energy, reflecting a limited power generation duration16–18, particularly in terms of current duration5. Current efforts to improve device lifespan include developing numerous strategies to maintain or enhance water and ion concentration gradients, such as constructing asymmetric or heterogeneous structures19,20, optimizing electrodes21,22, and engineering functional materials23. However, unidirectional ion migration leads to ion accumulation on one side of the device, generating an internal reverse electric field that impedes the movement of subsequent ions, thereby causing the device's power generation to decay. Some studies have attempted to introduce redox reactions to consume the ions accumulated at the electrodes, thereby mitigating the reverse electric field and enabling long-term power generation; however, electrode redox reactions should ideally be avoided in pure hydrovoltaic devices24. Our previous work achieved 600 h of power generation by introducing photocatalysis to consume accumulated hydrogen ions and restore the concentration gradient25, but this method requires an additional energy input and suffers from limited performance recovery after multiple cycles. Therefore, solving the lifetime issue requires new strategies that overcome the limitations of unidirectional ion transport and promote bidirectional ion transport.

For the moisture-induced ion-diffusion phenomenon, returning the migrated ions by introducing humidity fluctuations is expected to rebuild the ion concentration gradient, making it an effective method to restore power generation performance. However, when humidity fluctuates in the opposite direction, most power generation devices do not give rise to ionic back migration23,26,27. This is because the moisture adsorption power generation driven by ion concentration difference and the moisture desorption power generation dominated by ion hydration take place in the same direction28. In very few studies, humidity fluctuations have been observed to induce ionic back migration29,30. For example, Zhao et al. noticed that the moisture adsorption/desorption process resulted in a water content difference in the transmembrane ionic liquid layer, which triggered a bidirectional transmembrane ionic flux, enabling the generation of an AC electrical signal for continuous energy harvesting30. However, the ion channel membranes described above demand a fine mesopore size and an average membrane thickness of 74 nm. The block copolymerization fabrication technology utilized has the disadvantages of high synthesis difficulty and harsh reaction conditions30,31, which will limit its promotion in practical applications. Further efforts are still required to explore new materials and mechanisms for ionic back-migration, thereby enabling sustainable power generation through the daily cycle of humidity.

In this work, we propose that the dynamic coordination between I- and I2 to synthesize I3- is regulated by external humidity fluctuations. In principle, this enables perpetual reconstruction of iodide ion concentrations and reciprocal ion migration driven by natural humidity cycles, without any external energy input. Based on this mechanism, we designed a hydrogel-based sustainable moisture-electric generator (SMEG). The upper surface of the SMEG is exposed to the air, while the lower surface and the surrounding area are isolated from the air (Fig. 1a). Under humidity fluctuations, I- ions in SMEG undergo continuous oscillatory migration, resulting in the sustained AC power generation. Detailed power generation processes are provided in Supplementary Fig. 1. The process of I- ions oscillation migration induced by moisture absorption and desorption was confirmed by a combination of electrical experimental tests, Raman spectroscopy, and theoretical calculations. Compared to traditional MEGs, our SMEG has excellent stability and sustained power generation capabilities. As shown in Fig. 1b, our device can continuously and stably generate electricity for nearly two weeks without performance degradation under the high-low humidity switching environment simulated in the laboratory (25±3 °C). Furthermore, even after being stored under laboratory conditions for seven months (30-65% RH, 25±3°C), the device was still able to operate continuously for one month (Supplementary Fig. 2), demonstrating its outstanding long-term storage stability and sustained performance exceeding one month. We tested four different hydrogels loaded with I3- ions, and all of them exhibited similar AC sustained power generation phenomena. This indicates that the power generation mechanism applies with minimal requirements for pore size and the chemical composition of the hydrogel skeleton material. Furthermore, our device exhibits excellent environmental adaptability, responding to small humidity fluctuations as low as 2% RH across a wide humidity range, demonstrating immense potential for continuous energy harvesting from ambient humidity variations. Overall, this work provides a mechanism and a material system for ion back-migration, offering an optimized platform for realizing stable, high-performance, and sustainable moisture-based electricity-generating devices.
paper_content.results:
Design and characterization of SMEG
The SMEG in question consists of a porous carbon upper electrode, a hydrogel functional layer surrounded by a sealing film and a carbon lower electrode (Fig. 1a). The hydrogel functional layer is composed of acrylamide (AM), 2-acrylamido-2-methylpropanesulfonic acid (AMPS) and sodium iodide (NaI) (Fig. 2a). AM mainly serves to provide structural support and improve water retention (Supplementary Fig. 3), while AMPS with sulphonic acid groups enables the functional layer to dissociate hydrogen ions through interaction with water molecules32–34. The use of a sealing film ensures that air contacts the functional layer from the top, facilitating the formation of ionic concentration differences. The introduction of NaI with medium hygroscopicity is the unique design of the functional layer, which allows endowing the device with three key properties:
(i) Due to the Hofmeister effect35–37, I- is a Chaotropic ion that makes the hydrogel skeleton more sparse, favoring ionic transport, and weakens the ion screening of the charged skeleton3,38,39.
(ii) NaI with appropriate hygroscopicity (Supplementary Fig. 4) provides the functional layer with excellent responsiveness to changes in humidity (absorption of moisture at relatively high humidity and desorption of moisture at relatively low humidity)40,41.
(iii) The following reactions occur in the acidic environment provided by the sulfonic acid group of AMPS, and the corresponding equations are as follows:
4I- + 4H+ + O2 = 2H2O + 2I2 (1)
I- + I2 ⇌ I3- (2)
In this case, Eq. (1) is the pre-reaction; Eq. (2) is a reversible dynamic coordination equilibrium, which is the core reaction of the power generation principle. The directionality of Eq. (2) is regulated by the water molecule content (humidity fluctuations) (for details, see the mechanism validation section). By comparing the microscopic morphologies of the NaI-treated and non-NaI-treated hydrogels, it is proven that the pore structure of the hydrogels becomes more sparse after the addition of I- (Fig. 2b,c). As seen in the inset of Fig. 2c, I3- is introduced into the hydrogel (the hydrogel changes from transparent to brown), confirming the presence of Eq. (2) and the generation of a large amount of I3- (I- itself is colorless and I3- is brown).

The entire device preparation process is described in the experimental section and supplementary information (Supplementary Fig. 5). To further illustrate the material properties, a series of characterizations were carried out on the moisture absorption/desorption, the distribution and type of iodine elements present in the hydrogel. Firstly, in addition to optimizing the hydrogel skeleton, NaI also provides good moisture absorption capacity, maintaining the hydrated state of the hydrogel. To demonstrate this, we compared the changes in hydrogels with and without NaI in an air environment (55% RH). The hydrogel without NaI becomes dried out and hardened after 48 h, whereas the one with NaI retains its original size even after being exposed to air for one month (Supplementary Fig. 6). At the same time, the moderate moisture uptake capacity of NaI enables the hydrogel to exhibit rapid moisture uptake and release behavior when switching between high humidity and low humidity (using a hydrogel thickness of 3 mm). As shown in Fig. 2d, a piece of gel was first pre-treated by placing it in a humidity chamber at 15% RH for 12 h, and then placed at 98% RH and 15% RH for 12 h, respectively, showing its good humidity responsiveness (Fig. 2d).

Secondly, the NaI distribution is analyzed by an Energy Dispersive Spectrometer (EDS) (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 7), and the iodine and sodium elements are evenly distributed throughout the hydrogel, confirming the uniform loading of NaI on its skeleton. Furthermore, iodine exists in three forms within the gel: I-, I2, and I3-. In the hydrated state, the laser Raman spectra confirms the presence of I3- and I2 (Supplementary Fig. 8)42–44. Additionally, the X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) of the dried hydrogel demonstrates that the hydrogel contains I3-, I2, and I- (Fig. 2f)45,46, with I3- having the highest proportion (Supplementary Table 1). This is consistent with our hypothesis that Eq. (2) tends to synthesize I3- under low humidity conditions. In summary, the hydrogel possesses the pore structure necessary for rapid ion mobility, good moisture uptake and release capabilities, and the dynamic coordination of I- and I2 to synthesize I3- is the key to device performance and power generation mechanism.

Electrical output performance and influencing factors of SMEG
The current signal associated with a large humidity switch (15% RH-98% RH) within 24 h reaches 33.2 µA at 98% RH changes reversely to −31.4 µA at 15% RH (Fig. 3a). Since the effective working area of the device is 1 cm2, the current density value is numerically equal to the current value. When the humidity is switched, the current amplitude displays a rapid increase, followed by a gradual decay. At the inception of environment switching, the rate of moisture absorption and desorption is the highest, thus engendering a comparatively substantial I- concentration difference and a rapid increase in current. As time elapses, the water exchange between the device and the environment is progressively balanced, the rate of moisture absorption and desorption diminishes, and the ionic motion slows down, consequently leading to a gradual decline in the device’s performance.

Subsequently, the influences of a series of preparation parameters on the power generation performance of the SMEG are studied. Firstly, the effect of NaI solution concentration is investigated, where the solution soaking time is fixed at 24 h (Fig. 3b). The results show that the device has optimal performance output when the NaI concentration is 1 M. In the case where the NaI concentration is 0.01 M, the device generates almost no electricity due to an insufficient number of ions participating in dynamic coordination. Conversely, when the NaI concentration is excessively high, the performance also deteriorates. This attenuation phenomenon may be attributed to the high concentration of NaI that tend to form ion pairs and the high osmotic pressure-induced dehydration or even collapse of the gel skeleton47–50, thus hindering ion transport (Supplementary Figs. 9 and 10). In the subsequent investigation, the concentration of NaI solution is fixed at 1 M, while the soaking time in NaI is varied. The impact of soaking time on device performance is shown in Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 11a. The overall trend shows that the output performance increases with soaking time and gradually reaches saturation. This is likely because the gel gradually absorbs more NaI, approaching its maximum absorption capacity over time (Supplementary Fig. 12). The sulfonic acid groups of AMPS dissociate hydrogen ions when interacting with water molecules, which promotes the formation of I2. Thus, the effect of different AMPS contents on the device performance is investigated (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 11b). The experimental results demonstrate that the device output current gradually increases with AMPS content before reaching a saturation plateau. This trend can be explained as follows: The sulfonic acid groups in AMPS provide additional H+ ions, which facilitate the conversion of I- to I3-, thereby enhancing device performance. However, when the H+ concentration reaches a certain threshold, the conversion between I- and I3- approaches equilibrium. Beyond this point, further increases in AMPS content no longer significantly promote I3- generation, resulting in the observed current stabilization. The positive correlation between I3- content and current intensity, as clearly demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 13, provides compelling experimental evidence to support our proposed mechanism.

The effect of hydrogel thickness on the device performance is further investigated (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Fig. 11c). The device current generation gradually increases and reaches saturation with increasing thickness. At a thickness of 9 mm, the moisture absorbing current can reach up to 30 µA and the desorbing current up to −30.5 µA. There is no obvious improvement in performance with further increases in thickness, but the electrical output lasts longer. When the thickness is thin, rapid water saturation causes a low humidity gradient in the gel, and the ion flux is small, resulting in a weak electrical signal. When the thickness is greater than 9 mm, the humidity gradient and the hydrogel ion flux gradually reach saturation, so that the device performance gradually saturates. It is noted that the time for the device to reach the peak current after the humidity changes also increases with thickness (Supplementary Fig. 11d), which is due to the fact that the greater the thickness, the greater the distance over which the ions are transported. The voltage signals at different thicknesses are further examined (Supplementary Fig. 14a) and the voltage gradually augments with the increase in thickness. In particular, for devices of 9 mm thickness, voltage changes were recorded during a single humidity cycle, and the results showed a trend similar to that of current (Supplementary Fig. 14b). Subsequently, the internal resistance of the 9-mm-thick device was evaluated via its current-voltage characteristics. The results indicate that even at 15% relative humidity, SMEG maintains an internal resistance of 390 Ω (Supplementary Fig. 15a). It can be inferred that the relatively low internal resistance is unfavorable for the formation of a substantial ionic concentration gradient, which ultimately results in a smaller output voltage. On the other hand, the low voltage may also originate from the internal ionic distribution prior to humidity fluctuations. Under steady-state conditions, iodide ions remain homogeneously distributed within the gel. Although humidity fluctuations trigger dynamic coordination and regenerate a concentration gradient, the pre-existing uniform distribution may diminish the net ion separation, thereby constraining the maximum voltage that can be produced. To comprehensively assess the power-output characteristics of the device, we measured the power density under various external load resistances (Supplementary Fig. 15b). A maximum power density of 0.049 µW cm-2 was obtained.

Interestingly, as shown in Fig. 3a–e, we observed that the device performance during absorption and desorption varies: in some cases, the performance is similar, while in others, the absorption current is 1.5-2 times higher than the desorption current. This phenomenon may originate from the different I-/I3- ratios within the hydrogel, which in turn lead to differences in its absorption and desorption capacities. Consequently, the device exhibits distinct performance characteristics during the absorption and desorption processes. The detailed analysis is provided in Supplementary Notes 1-2 and Supplementary Figs. 13, 16 and 17. Furthermore, to further elucidate the role of the sealing film, we systematically varied the thickness of the gel layer to examine the influence of sealing films on device performance under 98% RH. As illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 18, devices with sealing films consistently exhibited superior performance compared to their unsealed counterparts. Notably, the performance gap between sealed and unsealed devices widened as the gel thickness increased. We attribute this phenomenon to the expanded lateral surface area of the gel exposed to ambient moisture at greater thicknesses, which reduces the ionic concentration gradient between the top and bottom electrodes, thereby degrading the electrical performance.

The humidity switching interval is another influencing factor (Fig. 3f), where the interval is the time between switching from 98% RH (15% RH) to 15% RH (98% RH). We compared three groups of switching intervals, and the reverse current amplitudes when high humidity turns to low humidity are extracted. The current of the device in the first group with an interval of 5 h is about −3 µA; the device current is up to −4.58 µA in the second group of 10 h intervals; the device current is up to −6.22 µA in the third group of 15 h intervals. The longer the humidity switching interval time, the higher the performance of the device can be recovered. This is because the longer the interval time, the more complete the Eq. (2) is. After switching the humidity, the ion concentration gradient in the reverse direction is larger, thus generating a larger current signal.

In addition, the influence of the number of holes in the top electrode on the electrical performance was also investigated, we conducted a series of experiments using top electrodes with different numbers of holes (5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 holes, each with a diameter of 1.5 mm) to investigate their influence on device performance during the humidification process. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 19, when the number of holes was small, the limited contact area with ambient moisture led to slower performance enhancement and lower peak output. In contrast, devices with a higher number of holes exhibited faster performance increase and higher peak currents, due to a larger exposed surface area facilitating more efficient moisture uptake. These findings are consistent with the proposed working mechanism.

Finally, we compared several recently reported MEGs, as summarized in Supplementary Table 2. The results indicate that the SMEG based on the dynamic-coordination-driven ion-concentration-reconstruction mechanism offers several key advantages, including a broad operational humidity range, the ability to be activated by small humidity variations, a low performance-decay rate, and robust long-term energy output. Concurrently, the maximum power density (VOC × JSC) of our device stands among the top tier when compared to other pure hydrovoltaic devices (i.e., those operating without electrode redox reactions). These features collectively underscore the strong potential of our device for sustainable and durable moisture-enabled energy generation.

Verification for electricity-generating mechanism
In order to explore the electricity-generating mechanism of the SMEG, the device electrical tests were first carried out under different moisture action modes (Fig. 4a). Four moisture action modes are considered: (i) moisture absorption/desorption on the upper surface of the device; (ii) moisture absorption/desorption on the lower surface of the device; (iii) moisture absorption/desorption on both surfaces of the device; (iv) sealing of the device on both sides. The results demonstrate that the devices operating under the first two asymmetric moisture action modes exhibit good power generation performance. In contrast, the current output is disordered when porous electrodes are employed on both the upper and lower surfaces. When the device is sealed on both sides, the current signal is negligible. The above phenomena prove that the power generation signal is closely related to the directional moisture absorption and desorption behavior of the device.

Secondly, to verify whether the observed AC generation originates from the hygroscopic nature of the salts, a range of hygroscopic salts (hygroscopicity of LiCl > CaCl2 > MgCl2 > NaI > NaF) were incorporated into the hydrogel41, and the power generation performance of the devices was examined at high and low humidity switching conditions (98% RH-15% RH) (Fig. 4b). Only the device with added NaI exhibits moisture absorption and desorption-induced AC power generation. When other types of hygroscopic salt devices switch between high humidity and low humidity, it will not reverse, although the current will fluctuate to a certain extent.

Since only the NaI-soaked hydrogel changes color, it is concluded that the AC generation phenomenon is related to the iodine element. Subsequently, various halogenated salts were added to the hydrogels for testing. The NaF, NaCl, and NaBr control devices exhibit no AC generation phenomenon, whereas the NaI-treated hydrogel demonstrates an AC electrical signal (Supplementary Fig. 20). Together with the observation that NaI-treated hydrogels turn brown, it indicates that the AC generation phenomenon is associated with the dynamic coordination between I- and I2 to form I3-, thereby underscoring the specificity of the element iodine. However, the limited contribution of Na+ to the power generation performance may be attributed to the fact that the migration of Na+ primarily relies on the movement of water molecules, whereas I- ions benefit from an additional driving force provided by the dynamic coordination process.

In order to elucidate the moisture absorption- and desorption-induced AC power generation phenomenon associated with elemental iodine, the following principle hypotheses are proposed. Firstly, two reactions occur during the immersion of P(AM-co-AMPS) hydrogels in NaI solution, creating prerequisites for device use (Refer to Eqs. (1) and (2) in section “Design and characterization of SMEG”). Secondly, the forward and reverse directions of the Eq. (2) are regulated by humidity. Precisely, in a dry environment, Eq. (2) proceeds in the forward direction, I- and I2 tend to coordinate to synthesize I3-; in a humid environment, Eq. (2) proceeds in the reverse direction, I3- tends to dissociate into I2 and I-. This humidity-modulated dynamic coordination serves as the core driving force for the device’s power generation. On this basis, when the device is switched from a low-humidity environment (15% RH) to a high-humidity environment (98% RH), the dissociation of I3- occurs on the air-contacting side of the device surface to produce I2 and I-, which contributes to a decrease in the concentration of I3- and an increase in the concentration of I-. However, considering that I- ions are smaller and move faster than I3- ions51,52, it is believed that the overall downward movement of I- that dominates the ionic current. The current will first increase and then decrease gradually to a near-zero level. This decrease is due to the gradual equilibration of the dynamic coordination. Concurrently, the voltage also shows an increase first and then a decrease next, illustrating a similar change pattern as electric current (Supplementary Fig. 14b). When the device is switched from a high humidity environment (98% RH) to a low humidity environment (15% RH), I- and I2 synthesize into I3- in the surface layer on the air-contacting side of the functional layer, prompting I- to flow back. This reciprocating oscillation of I- enables the device to generate electricity continuously.

To validate Eqs. (1) and (2), we compared the power generation differences of hydrogels with different AMPS contents in the previous section, proving the importance of the acid environment induced by the dissociation of protons from the AMPS sulfonate group. To further confirm the contribution of hydrogen ions, we immersed PAM gels in NaI solution with added HCl, and the device power generation performance was restored to a level comparable to that of the P(AM-co-AMPS)-NaI hydrogel device (Fig. 4c). In contrast, the PAM-NaI control device showed very weak power generation phenomenon without HCl addition, indicating the importance of I3- to the moisture-induced AC power generation phenomenon. The above results strongly indicate the presence of Eq. (1), and the introduction of hydrogen ions changes the hydrogel color from transparent to dark brown, confirming the presence of I3- and Eq. (2).

Further, to illustrate the generalizability of the dynamic coordination strategy, hydrogels with different backbone charges, namely P(AM-co-AMPS), PAM, poly[2-(methacryloyloxy)ethyl] trimethyl ammonium chloride (PMETAC), ploy[2-(methacryloyloxy)ethyl] dimethyl-(3-sulfonatopropyl) ammonium hydroxide (PDMAPS), were immersed in NaI and NaI (HCl), respectively. The hydrogel devices immersed in NaI (HCl) all show similar AC signals (Fig. 4d), indicating that the dynamic coordination strategy is universal and has low requirements for gel backbone materials. The small difference in the amplitude of the electrical signals under different charged skeletons maybe due to the salt-in effect of NaI, which loosens the hydrogel skeleton. A higher salt concentration shorten the Debay length and inhibits the electrical screening of the charged skeleton by the bilayer.

The ion transport dynamic originates mainly from moisture absorption- and desorption-induced I- concentration gradients rather than interfacial charge modulation. When PAM, PMETAC, and PDMAPS are immersed in acid-free NaI, the hydrogel currents show very weak oscillations (Supplementary Fig. 21). This may be due to the introduction of a small amount of I3- during the heat treatment of the prepared devices, giving the device AC power generation capability. Taking PAM hydrogel as an example, it can be seen that the hydrogel remains transparent after being immersed in NaI, and becomes slightly yellow (Supplementary Fig. 22) after heat treatment, indicating the introduction of a small amount of I3-. The yellowing may be attributed to the partial ionization of water molecules within the hydrogel, generating a small amount of H+, which then reacts with I- to form a trace amount of I3-.

To verify that the dynamic coordination equilibrium is regulated by humidity, we performed Raman characterization on the PAM-AMPS hydrogel in different humidity environments (Fig. 4e). The hydrogel was tested after being placed in a 15% RH humidity chamber for 12 h. Raman intensity maps relevant to I3- at ≈110 cm-1 are shown (Fig. 4e-I). Next, the hydrogel was placed in a 98% RH humidity chamber for 30 min, and the laser Raman test was performed again. An overall weakening of the peak intensity of I3- is found (Fig. 4e-II), indicating a decrease in the content of I3- and proving that I3- tends to dissociate under high humidity. Further, the hydrogel was transferred to a 15% RH humidity chamber for 30 min, and the Raman test was performed again. The results show that the concentration of I3- becomes high again (Fig. 4e-III). Subsequently, the continuous and dynamic evolution of the Raman spectra of the hydrogel was monitored during humidity switching cycles, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 23. The results obtained after transferring the sample from a 15% RH humidity chamber to the laboratory ambient environment for testing are shown in Supplementary Fig. 23a. These data reveal a gradual decrease in I3- concentration from its initially high level, providing strong evidence that I3- dissociates into I2 and I- during the moisture-absorption process. Conversely, after placing the sample in a 98% RH humidity chamber for 30 min and then transferring it back to the laboratory ambient environment for Raman characterization, the results shown in Supplementary Fig. 23b demonstrate that I3- is regenerated when the hydrogel undergoes moisture desorption. The experiments performed provide strong evidence that the Eq. (2) is regulated by humidity.

To further demonstrate that Eq. (2) is regulated by humidity, we carried out theoretical calculations. Two conditions were setup for simulation analysis, one for the dissociation of I3- under water-rich condition and the other under water-poor condition. The dissociation of I3- under water-rich condition was analyzed using the NEB method (Fig. 4f). In this case, I3- is wrapped with 44 water molecule explicit solvent shell and the outer layer is treated with an implicit solvent model. The results show that the dissociation energy barrier in the presence of an aqueous solvent is 18.2 kcal/mol, which can be significantly carried out at room temperature. To provide a clearer understanding of the dissociation behavior of the I3- and its interaction with surrounding water molecules, we provided an illustration of the I3- dissociation pathway (see Supplementary Fig. 24). In contrast, scanning using a flexible surface under solvent-free condition yields a dissociation energy barrier of up to 23.36 kcal/mol (Fig. 4g), which is too slow to proceed at room temperature. Combined with the scan path trends, the water explicit and implicit solvent models reduce the dissociation energy barrier between I- and I2 to a reasonable range compared to the anhydrous solvent case, so that I3- is able to dissociate smoothly in water-rich environments. It becomes kinetically more favorable to dissociate I3- in water because the I3- → I- + I2 reaction is a single molecule reaction (first-order rate constant), whereas the I- + I2 → I3- inverse reaction is a bi-molecule reaction (second-order rate constant). In a water-poor or anhydrous environment, it is difficult to cross the energy barrier at room temperature due to the high energy barrier, and thus the reaction always tends to return to I3-. Since the reverse process in the water-rich state (Fig. 4f, looking from right to left) need to overcome a small energy barrier, and this energy barrier gives I- the opportunity to escape at water enrichment. For the energy curve calculated in the anhydrous environment, the path is reversed to see that there is almost no energy barrier, and it is a direct monotonic energy drop, which makes I- escape after coming out and follow the energy curve back to the reactants. Therefore, the calculation results also support the hypothesis that Eq. (2) is regulated by humidity.

Environment-adaptive applications
The cyclic change in humidity caused by the diurnal cycle in daily life is a reliable source of energy. For example, on a sunny day, the humidity reaches a maximum on the eve of sunrise and gradually decreases to a minimum as the sun rises; then the humidity rises slowly as the sun sets and night falls, repeating this cycle (Fig. 5a). Given the above scenario, we simulated the process in a temperature and humidity chamber in order to better observe the response of the device to humidity, with the temperature set at 25 °C and the humidity varying cyclically from 40-90% RH in a cycle of 12 h (Fig. 5b). The current curve of the device in the above environment is also recorded, and the results show that the device is very sensitive to humidity changes and generates power cyclically with the humidity cycle. In addition, we conducted experiments to assess the device’s performance under real outdoor environmental conditions (Supplementary Fig. 25). The results confirm that the device can effectively respond to ambient humidity fluctuations and continuously generate electricity, thereby underscoring the practical potential of SMEG.

Further, small-amplitude humidity fluctuations are also frequently encountered in real-world environments. To assess the performance of SMEG under such practical conditions, we first examined its current response under modest humidity variations. As shown in Fig. 5c, the device maintains stable and reproducible switching behavior, demonstrating a high degree of adaptability even when the humidity change is relatively minor. To further evaluate the sensitivity limit of the device, we investigated its response to extremely small humidity perturbations. Remarkably, SMEG can reliably detect variations as low as 2% RH, underscoring its exceptional responsiveness and broad applicability across diverse humidity conditions (Supplementary Fig. 26; Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Meanwhile, we evaluated the device's oscillatory energy-generating behavior under these small humidity fluctuations. As presented in Fig. 5d, SMEG continues to exhibit AC-type power generation even when the humidity varies by only 13-14% RH under both high-humidity and low-humidity conditions. This capability highlights the device’s strong environmental adaptability and confirms that dynamic coordination-driven ion oscillation remain effective over narrow humidity ranges.
paper_content.methods:
Chemicals and materials
Unless otherwise stated, all reagents and solvents were used without further purification. Acrylamide (AM, Macklin), 2-acrylamido-2-methylpropanesulfonic acid (AMPS, Sigma-Aldrich), N,N′-methylene bisacrylamide (MBAA, Sigma-Aldrich), 2-hydroxy-4’-(2-hydroxyethoxy)-2-methylpropiophenone (Irgacure 2959, Aladdin), [2-(methacryloyloxy)ethyl] trimethylammonium chloride (METAC, Aladdin), [2-(methacryloyloxy)ethyl] dimethyl-(3-sulfonatopropyl) ammonium hydroxide (DMAPS, HEOWNS), and lithium chloride (LiCl, Sigma-Aldrich). Calcium chloride, magnesium chloride, sodium iodide, potassium iodide, sodium bromide, sodium chloride, sodium fluoride, and hydrochloric acid were analytically pure and purchased from Chengdu Kelong Chemical Co., Ltd. Hydrochloric acid was diluted to 1 M for use.

The preparation process of SMEG
a) Preparation of hydrogel precursor solution and gel: Firstly, weigh the gel monomer AM (6 g), AMPS (x g, where x = 0, 0.7, 1.4, 2.1, 2.8, 3.5, 4.2 or 4.9), the crosslinking agent MBAA (15 mg), and the initiator Irgacure 2959 (15 mg). Put the above materials into 30 mL of deionized water, and stir for 20 min with a magnetic stirrer at room temperature until all are dissolved. The precursor solution was added dropwise into a mold (the mold size can be customized), and the precursor solution was irradiated by a UV lamp with a power of 30 W for 20 min to prepare a hydrogel successfully. The preparation of PEMEATC and PDMAPS did not require using AM, and the other steps remained unchanged.
b) Introduction of NaI: it was sufficient to soak the prepared hydrogel in NaI solution for 48 h.
c) Water content control of the gel: the soaked gel was placed in a drying oven at 80 °C for about 3 h, and then placed in the atmosphere or a specified humidity environment for 12 h to wait for its moisture absorption and desorption equilibrium (i.e., the volume was similar to that of the original gel, or no longer changed significantly).
d) Electrode preparation and assembly: Carbon electrodes were prepared by commercial carbon paste coated on PET film, waiting for its natural drying to be used. The porous electrodes were prepared by using a laser marking machine to punch holes with a diameter of 1.5 mm and a spacing of 0.4 mm, totaling 5 × 5 holes. Conductive carbon tape was used to connect the carbon fiber leads to the carbon electrodes, and the carbon fiber leads were sealed with transparent tape to prevent liquid condensed on the sidewall of the humidity chamber from entering the carbon fiber leads. Two carbon electrodes were placed on both sides of the hydrogel, the top electrode was a porous carbon electrode and the bottom electrode was a normal carbon electrode. The perimeter of the gel was sealed by a sealing film, and the effective working area of the device is 1 cm2. The detailed process is shown in Supplementary Fig. 5.

Material characterization
The cross-sectional morphology of the gel was characterized by field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Apreo 2C, Thermo Fisher, US). Elemental analyses in the gel-dried state were made by an EDS unit attached to the SEM instrument and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (K-Alpha, Thermo Scientific, US). XPS data were analyzed using Avantage 6.6.0 and plotted with Origin 2024. The triiodide ion characterization of gels in the water-containing state was performed using a laser confocal Raman spectrometer (Horiba, Japan), which was tested in ambient laboratory conditions (55% RH, 25 °C), a laser of 532 nm, and a laser intensity of 3.2%. Raman mapping data were analyzed using LabSpec 6 software.

Electrical measurements
Half a month of data was obtained using a semiconductor parameter analyzer (Keithley 4200A-SCS). Short-time currents and voltages were recorded using a digital source meter (Keithley 2450). The circuit parameter for the open circuit voltage test was a current of 0 nA, and the circuit parameter for the short circuit current test was a voltage of 0 V. Current-voltage characteristics were measured using an electrochemical analyzer (CHI760E, CH Instruments, USA) with a voltage window of −10 mV to 10 mV and a scan rate of 1 mV/s. All electrical data were analyzed and plotted using Origin 2024.

Temperature and humidity conditions for electrical measurements
Except for the experiments shown in Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 25, all other tests were conducted in humidity chambers provided by saturated salt solutions40,53, with the laboratory temperature maintained at 25 ± 3 °C. Temperature and humidity variations in the simulated environment provided by the constant temperature and humidity chamber (DHTHM-27-80-P-SD) in Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 26. The humidity of the real environment was recorded by a Rotronic hygrometer (Rotronic Hygrolog NT, Switzerland) with a sampling interval of 5 s.

Theoretical calculation Methods
All calculations were performed using the ORCA version 6.0 program package54 with BLYP55,56-D3BJ57,58 functions and the ma59-def2-SVP60 basis set. The ma-def2-SVP basis set was chosen because of the anionic nature of I- and its explicitly soluble droplets. The def2/J61 auxiliary basis set was also used. Pure functions combined with the resolved identity (RI)62 approximation were used to model explicitly solvated I3- systems consisting of 135 atoms (44 water molecules explicit solvent shells and three iodine atoms) and a large number of hydrogen bonds. A water density (SMD)63-based solvation model was used as an implicit solvation model outside of the explicit solvent shell. The cleavage and dissociation of I3- were simulated by relaxation surface scanning, since the reaction does not have an effective product equilibrium geometry (a smooth decrease in energy after an energy barrier). The calculations were performed without using any solvation model to simulate systems with little water content. In contrast, the explicitly solvated I3- was analyzed using the naked elastic band (NEB)64 method with climb images to determine the minimum energy reaction path for its cleavage and dissociation.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this work, Lu et al. studied the moisture-based energy harvesting through oscillatory migration of ions driven by humidity fluctuations-induced dynamic coordination. This research work is somewhat meaningful and interesting. However, this article has many aspects that need improvement. Many further experiments and explanation should be included in the revision. Here are the comments.
1. It seemed that the authors controlled the humidity fluctuations in a humidity chamber and the humidity ranged from the 15% to 98%. What was the temperature for the test? Was the measurement conducted under variable temperature condition or constant temperature condition? The authors did not provide any details on this point in the Methods part. This is quite unrigorous.
2. Influence of some optimized synthesis preparation was strange. In Figure 3b, why did the current decrease when the NaI concentration was higher than 1 M? It was hard to understand. In Figure 3c, for the different soaking time, why did the current decrease at 24 h but increase at 48 h for desorption? These results should be well explained in the manuscript.
3. In the proposed mechanism, the reaction 4I-+4H++O2=2H2O+2I2 was not reversible. This hinted that I- ions would be continuously consumed. That was to say, when the I- ions completely converted to I2, the device would not work. How many adsorption/desorption circles could the device operate?
4. In Figure 1b, why the current in the adsorption process was always larger than that in desorption process?
5. What was the NaI adsorption capacity or the content in the hydrogel? This should be also measured. It seemed that the NaI content in the hydrogel would influence the current.
6. Actually I2 will also slowly evaporate through sublimation at room temperature. This means that the I2 in the hydrogel will slowly decrease. Would the authors observe a decline in current after long-term performance measurements?
7. Why the Na+ ion cannot be transported in hydrogel? This is essential and should be discussed in the revised manuscript.
8. What about the open circuit potential for the device at steady state? Corresponding measurement is missing.
9. In Figure 4e, the Raman intensity maps of P(AM-co-AMPS)-NaI gel in different humidity environments were displayed. The authors mentioned that it was placed in a “humidity bottle”. What was the “humidity bottle”? I was curious about that how the authors perform the Raman characterizations in different humidity environments. Corresponding experimental conditions need to be put in the Methods parts.
10. Some minor errors need to be noted. There should be a space between the number and the unit. Please check.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript, entitled " Humidity fluctuations-induced dynamic coordination drives the oscillatory migration of ions for sustainable energy harvesting" introduces a hydrogel-based sustainable moisture-electric generator (SMEG) based on the dynamic coordination between I- and I2 to synthesize I3-. Specifically, the authors reasonably demonstrated through Raman spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations that the dynamic coordination is regulated by the adsorption and desorption of moisture, endowing it with the ability to continuously operate in an environment with cyclic changes in air humidity. It has been tested to be able to work stably for nearly two weeks in a simulated environmental chamber. In general, the concept of ion oscillation migration driven by dynamic coordination is novel and impressive. It has shown remarkable potential for enabling the continuous and stable operation of moisture-based energy-harvesting devices. However, several concerns need to be addressed before it can be published in Nature communications. Please see the following detailed comments.
[Comment 1] In line 24, the abstract states that “The coordination process of I- does not involve charge exchange, and the charge transfer behavior (electricity generation) is still achieved through moisture-driven ion transport.” However, the text appears to lack corresponding evidence for this claim. Please provide a detailed explanation of this behavior.
[Comment 2] In line 70, the definitions of relative high humidity and low humidity are not clearly delineated in the preceding text. Please provide a specific explanation for these terms.
[Comment 3] In line 105, it is mentioned that “The use of a sealing film ensures that air contacts the functional layer from the top, facilitating the formation of ionic concentration differences.” However, what is the performance of the device when there is no sealing film around it? This could be further elucidated through a control experiment, which would help to corroborate the working mechanism of the device.
[Comment 4] In line 112, it is stated that the material possesses a moderate hygroscopic capacity. However, the degree of this hygroscopic capacity is not specifically described, and the current description is somewhat vague. It is recommended to supplement the text with comparative data on the hygroscopic capacities of commonly used adsorbents.
[Comment 5] In line 258, the ranking of the hygroscopic capabilities of different salts is provided without experimental evidence or reference to relevant literature. It is necessary to supplement this by either conducting experiments to measure the hygroscopic properties of the salts or by citing pertinent studies that have previously reported such rankings.
[Comment 6] In line 262, the power generation effects of hydrogels treated with other salt solutions are mentioned, but the underlying mechanisms for each are not explained. It is suggested to provide a brief explanation of the working principles for these cases.
[Comment 7] During the device fabrication process, what is the impact of the drying temperature of the hydrogel on the gel properties, and why was 80°C specifically chosen?
[Comment 8] It is suggested to enlarge a single cycle of data in Fig. 1b to more clearly highlight the characteristics of the data.
[Comment 9] Why do Fig. 3b and 3c exhibit significant differences in forward and reverse current performance, while the forward and reverse currents in Fig. 3a are at the same level?
[Comment 10] In Fig. 3d, it is suggested to further increase the content of AMPS and measure the corresponding current performance to see if the current continues to decrease. Adding one or two more data points would make the trend more evident.
[Comment 11] The curves in Fig. 4a are recommended to be labeled with numbers or letters for differentiation. The current presentation is not conducive to reader comprehension.
[Comment 12] It is suggested to provide a comparative table of similar devices (including aspects such as lifetime, humidity range, and working principles) to highlight the advantages of this device. The current presentation relies solely on textual descriptions, which lacks intuitiveness.
[Comment 13] The performance of the device under real environmental conditions is missing. It is recommended to supplement the curves showing the device's current performance fluctuating with humidity in a real atmospheric environment to demonstrate its working state under actual conditions.
[Comment 14] In Fig. 5d, only two sets of humidity difference data are provided. It is suggested to supplement with additional data points.
[Comment 15] It is recommended to include images showing the relationship between the number of breathable pores in the top electrode and the performance changes, in order to illustrate the correlation between the contact area of moisture and the device performance.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Comments:
Lu et al. proposed a novel moisture-electricity conversion mechanism based on the dynamic coordination between iodine ions and iodine molecules to keep a continuous ions migration for a long operating lifespan in MEG. While this strategy exhibits promising extensibility to diverse functional materials and broad humidity adaptability, its practical implementation faces notable limitations. The material only achieves voltage (~0.2 V) and current density (~33 μA/cm2) performance even at extremely high humidity environment (98%RH), which is an order of magnitude lower than recent related literature (Nat Commun 15, 3329 (2024), Nat Commun 15, 6100 (2024)). In addition, more evidence is needed to understand the mechanism by which this material generates electrical signals in a humidity environment. Therefore, in my opinion, this manuscript can be accepted after major revisions for publishing in Nature Communications.
1. Currently, most MEG studies based on functional hydrogels attribute the generation of electrical signals to the dissociation of protons (H⁺) from functional groups and their migration along the concentration gradient. However, this manuscript uses NaI to neutralize the dissociated hydrogen ions and uses the migration of negatively charged ions to generate electrical signals. Therefore, the gradient within the SMEG must be inferior to the previous one, resulting in a weaker electrical signal, which is also demonstrated by the performance in the manuscript. Given this significant performance gap, the proposed mechanism may offer limited advancement for the field.
2. Figure 1b shows that the SMEG has high cycling stability. However, the reversible reaction is difficult to maintain the ion gradient, as evidenced by the significant current decay from 10 μA to 2 μA within 24 hours. The positive and negative jumps of the electrical signal caused by the adsorption-desorption switching also limit the practical application scenarios of SMEG.
3. In Line 52-54, the authors mentioned ‘… the moisture desorption power generation dominated by ion hydration take place in the same direction’. Iodide ions also appear to form hydrates. How did the authors exclude this factor from their explanation?
4. While the proposed mechanism identifies PAMPS and NaI as the key functional components in the SMEG system, the rationale for using P(AM-co-AMPS) as the polymer matrix remains unclear. Although the authors note PAM's hydrophilic nature, this alone does not sufficiently justify its incorporation into the copolymer structure. Does PAM actively participate in power generation, or does it just play a role as a structural support? In what ways do P(AM-co-AMPS) copolymers have advantages over pure PAMPS?
5. The coordinates on the right side of Figure 2D seem to be wrong, as desorption and adsorption should be a continuous process in this figure. Did the authors mean to say desorption rate (%)?
6. In Figures 3b and c, the current during adsorption is 1.5 to 2 times that during desorption, whereas in other variables studied, the current during adsorption and desorption are similar. The authors should explain this.
7. In Line 286-288, the authors mentioned that ‘However, since I3- moves much slower than I-, it is the overall downward movement of I- that dominates the ionic current (Fig.4a)’. Figure 4A does not seem to justify this statement. The authors should add more evidence to demonstrate the difference in diffusion rates between I3- and I- in the material.
8. In Figure 4b, why are the positive and negative signs of the current signals of CaCl2 and LiCl opposite?
9. In Figure 4c, the authors compared different hydrogels with NaI, and found that PAM-NaI generate almost no current. Based on the mechanistic explanation in the manuscript, it can be speculated that this is because there is no release of hydrogen ions. However, previous literatures (Energy Environ. Sci., 2024, 17, 3788-3796, Nano Energy, 2024, 110590) has demonstrated that PAM also releases and migrates hydrogen ions during moisture adsorption, thereby producing current. The authors should clarify this discrepancy.
10. The font of ‘°C’ in Figure 5b seems to be different from other words. And I suggest that the author use ‘h’ instead of ‘s’ for the horizontal axis.
11. The language of the manuscript should be improved. Many prepositions are used incorrectly. For example, in line 184-185, ‘… NaI concentration is of 0.01 M, …’ should be ‘…NaI concentration is 0.01 M…’ and ‘participating in the dynamic coordination’ should be ‘participating in dynamic coordination’.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The authors design and fabricate a sustainable power generator SMEG based on the dynamic coordination of I- induced by varying humidity. The device shows great potential in small-scale green and sustainable energy access. However, there are several concerns that must be addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication:
1. Figure 3d shows that the performance is the best when the AMPS content is 2.8g, but it does not explain why excessive AMPS reduces the performance.
2. The Raman intensity maps in Figure 4e do not give the color scale annotation.
3. Explain in detail how moisture leads to the alternating changes in the I- concentration.
4. The principal comparison between moisture power generators and other novel power generation strategies should be added to the introduction.
5. The moisture power generator reported in this work should be compared with the literature to demonstrate its advantages.
6. A theoretical analysis should be given on whether the dynamic mechanism based on I- can be extended to other halogen ions.

[Response] We sincerely thank you for this critical question. Theoretically speaking,
increasing the concentration of NaI should provide more I- ions for migration, which
would be beneficial to the device’s output performance. However, we observed that the
optimal performance was achieved at a NaI concentration of 1 M, while a further
increase to 2 M led to a decrease in output. This counterintuitive behavior can be
understood by the Hofmeister effect.
Indeed, I- is a typical chaotropic ion, which, at moderate concentrations, can
significantly enhance hydrogen bonding between water molecules and the polymer
network. This increases the solubility of the gel, making its structure more swollen and
water-rich, which in turn facilitates ion migration and diffusion. As reported by Swann
et al.1, I- can markedly promote the swelling behavior of pH-responsive hydrogels
within a certain concentration range.
However, when the NaI concentration increases beyond the optimal range, the
chaotropic effect diminishes or even reverses. This is primarily due to two factors2-4:
(1) At high concentrations, Na+ and I- ions are more likely to form ion pairs,
reducing the proportion of free iodide ions available for migration;
(2) The high ionic strength leads to increased osmotic pressure, which can induce
dehydration or compression of the hydrogel network, thereby hindering ion transport.
Our experimental results suggest that at 1 M NaI, an optimal balance is achieved
among ion concentration, hydration effect, and gel structure, leading to the best power
output. This observation aligns well with the current understanding of the
concentration-dependent Hofmeister effect.
To further verify this, we performed SEM characterization of the hydrogel
network at 2 M NaI, which clearly revealed that high salt concentrations compromise
the polymer structure (Supplementary Fig. 10), impairing ion transport.
Additionally, in response to your comment on Fig. 3c, we repeated the experiments.
We found that the performance drop after 24 h immersion was due to individual device
issues. The overall trend shows that the output performance increases with soaking time
and gradually reaches saturation. This is likely because the gel gradually adsorbs more
NaI, approaching its maximum adsorption capacity over time (Supplementary Fig. 12).
We sincerely thank you for your comment, which helped us more clearly interpret
the underlying causes of this phenomenon.
We have refined the explanation of the relevant phenomena in the revised
manuscript.

From the foregoing table, it can be concluded that in most current moisture-enabled power generation devices, the primary mechanism is humidity-induced directional ion migration. In some high-performance devices, redox reactions may also play a role. While the direct current (DC) generation mode based on directional ion migration offers the advantage of easy direct utilization, it relies on a limited supply of mobile ions, which imposes a theoretical limit on its operational lifetime and often results in rapid performance degradation.
In contrast, the alternating current (AC) generation mode can continuously re-establish ion concentration gradients through external humidity fluctuations.
Theoretically speaking, this enables perpetual power generation with a significantly lower degradation rate. Therefore, the working mode demonstrated in this study highlights a theoretical advantage in the context of sustainable power generation.

[Comment 1] Currently, most MEG studies based on functional hydrogels attribute the
generation of electrical signals to the dissociation of protons (H⁺) from functional
groups and their migration along the concentration gradient. However, this manuscript
uses NaI to neutralize the dissociated hydrogen ions and uses the migration of
negatively charged ions to generate electrical signals. Therefore, the gradient within
the SMEG must be inferior to the previous one, resulting in a weaker electrical signal,
which is also demonstrated by the performance in the manuscript. Given this significant
performance gap, the proposed mechanism may offer limited advancement for the field.
[Response] We are very grateful for your in-depth comparative analysis of our work
with traditional proton migration-based hydrovoltaic power generation mechanisms.
Indeed, most current hydrogel-based MEG studies attribute the generation of electrical
signals to the directional migration of H+ released by acidic groups driven by
concentration gradients. In our work, we used NaI to neutralize the dissociated H+ in
the material. In addition, in view the inherent humidity fluctuations in the natural
atmospheric environment, we focused on the ion migration behavior caused by the
dynamic coordination of iodine by humidity fluctuations so as to explore a new ion
migration driving mechanism. It is expected to utilize the inherent day and night
humidity fluctuations in nature to achieve long-lasting performance output.
We fully recognize that the overall output performance of our device is indeed
lower than that of the proton-dominated system due to the suppression of high-mobility
proton participation. However, we believe that this dynamic coordination-driven ion
oscillation migration mechanism is still of great significance for the following reasons:
1. Provide a new perspective on ion migration mechanism: By introducing
iodine anion migration instead of traditional H⁺ migration, we have broadened the
research scope of humidity-responsive ion transport mechanism, which is particularly
suitable for some application scenarios where it is not suitable or desirable to introduce
protons (such as systems with high requirements for material chemical stability).
2. Provide a driving force for theoretical sustainable power generation: Most
traditional devices are DC power generation modes, relying on ion concentration
gradients to drive ion unidirectional movement. However, the concentration gradient of
most devices is difficult to maintain and rebuild, or additional energy is required to re-
establish the concentration gradient to make the device work again. The dynamic
coordination mechanism driven by moisture fluctuations will theoretically continuously
output electrical energy in the natural environment without the need for other additional
energy input.
3. Provide a basis for subsequent performance optimization: Although the
current output is still at a low level, we believe that this strategy has laid the foundation
for the construction of a moisture sustainable power generation system, and has room
for further optimization of performance by building directional ion channels and
improving ion mobility.
At the same time, the significant performance difference may be caused by
inefficient ion transport and interface charge conversion. Our subsequent work will
draw on some excellent strategies to further improve device performance, mainly
including the following aspects:
1. Device structure optimization: We plan to draw on technologies such as
directional freezing and cryogelation to construct a hydrogel network with directional
pore structure and strong deformation resistance. This type of structure helps the
efficient migration of ions under humidity gradients, and is expected to significantly
improve the current density and working stability of the device.
2. Improvement of interface charge conversion efficiency: We will modify the
surface nanostructure of the inert electrode surface (such as constructing a rough
structure of nanoparticles or introducing a microporous structure) to increase the
effective contact area of the electrode and reduce the interface impedance, thereby
improving the efficiency of ion and electron coupling; introduce an intermediate layer
material with high ion-electron coupling ability (such as PEDOT:PSS, etc.) between
the electrode and the gel. This type of materials has good charge transfer performance
and can effectively promote the efficient conversion of ions to electrons at the interface,
thereby ameliorating output stability and energy utilization efficiency.
3. Optimization of the internal ion system: On the basis of maintaining the non-
redox mechanism, we will explore ions or ion composite systems with higher mobility
and stronger polarizability to enhance the ion response rate and migration efficiency.
4. Exploitation of the temperature and humidity synergy: Considering that the
ambient temperature and humidity usually have coupled fluctuation characteristics, our
subsequent work attempts to design devices capable of exploiting the humidity
response mechanism and the energy of the ambient temperature so as to synergistically
promote device performance.
We believe that through the above multi-dimensional collaborative optimization
strategy, the performance of devices based on the moisture-driven dynamic
coordination mechanism can be significantly improved, and its practical applications
can be expanded.
In summary, although the current performance of our device cannot be compared
with the one of the mainstream MEGs based on the proton migration mechanism, the
conceptual exploration and new mechanism path it provides promote the diversified
development of theories and material systems in this field, while being extremely
valuable in the direction of sustainable power generation.
[Comment 2] Figure 1b shows that the SMEG has high cycling stability. However, the
reversible reaction is difficult to maintain the ion gradient, as evidenced by the
significant current decay from 10 μA to 2 μA within 24 hours. The positive and negative
jumps of the electrical signal caused by the adsorption-desorption switching also limit
the practical application scenarios of SMEG.
[Response] We thank you for pointing out that ion concentration is difficult to maintain.
This phenomenon is also a key research object in the field. Many papers have
introduced advanced strategies to enhance and maintain ion concentration gradients.
However, one highlight of our work is the proposition of a dynamic coordination-driven
ion oscillation migration mechanism induced by humidity fluctuations. Another
highlight is that the ion concentration gradient is reestablished through this mechanism
to achieve long-term stable operation of the device. Therefore, our strategy sacrifices
the maintenance of ion concentration and turns to the inherent moisture fluctuations in
the atmospheric environment to rebuild the concentration gradient through a reversible
dynamic coordination mechanism, which allows achieving long-term power generation.
Concerning the problem of positive and negative transitions in the electrical signal
output by the device during the adsorption-desorption switching process, note that,
since a moisture-based power generation device relies on environmental humidity
fluctuations to drive ion oscillation migration, it usually exhibits alternating electrical
signals that change with humidity cycles. Regarding the application of AC signals, we
explored feasible strategies for its applications with respect to the following aspects:
1. Signal regulation through rectification and energy storage unit: Low-
voltage rectification circuit (such as Schottky bridge rectification) and micro-
capacitor/supercapacitor can be integrated to achieve effective rectification and
smoothing of AC signals, thereby outputting stable DC voltage, which can be directly
used in low-power electronic devices (such as LEDs, sensors)20,21,23.
2. Use of humidity fluctuation signals for functional control or environmental
perception: We notice that positive and negative transitions actually reflect the periodic
fluctuations of ambient humidity, so the AC signal can be used as frequency encoding
or threshold trigger signals in some scenarios such as environmental perception and
intelligent control. For example, this periodic change can be applied in intelligent
ventilation, respiratory monitoring24, and humidity control systems.
3. Combining it with bionic circuits or AC adaptive systems: In recent years,
studies have used low-frequency AC signals in the fields of neural synapse simulation
and frequency-responsive sensors25,26. We believe that such signals can be expanded to
frequency-sensitive systems27 (such as soft electronics, skin electronics, etc.).
In summary, although the output signal of the SMEG has positive and negative
transitions, we believe that this feature is surmountable through optimization of
electronic circuit design, system integration, and functional application. In addition, it
has unique advantages in some specific applications.

[Comment 3] In Line 52-54, the authors mentioned ‘… the moisture desorption power
generation dominated by ion hydration take place in the same direction’. Iodide ions
also appear to form hydrates. How did the authors exclude this factor from their
explanation?
[Response] We sincerely thank you for raising this insightful question. Indeed, iodide
ions are known to form hydration shells, and the potential influence of ion hydration on
ions transport behavior cannot be entirely excluded. We appreciate the opportunity to
clarify this point further.
In our system, although hydration may provide a certain level of driving force, we
believe that the dominant driving factor for ion migration—particularly under humidity
fluctuations—is the ion concentration gradient. This judgment is based on both
physicochemical considerations and experimental evidence:
First, in terms of ion properties, iodide ions have a relatively large ionic radius (2.2
Å) and a lower charge density compared to smaller cations like sodium (1.02 Å).
Consequently, their electrostatic interaction with water molecules is weaker. Reported
hydration energies support this view: the hydration energy of Na+ is approximately –
365 kJ/mol, while that of I- is around -275 kJ/mol28. This suggests that iodide ions
experience a less pronounced hydration effect, and thus a relatively weaker hydration-
induced driving force.
Second, from the experimental perspective, if ion hydration were the main driving
force, the direction of ion migration (and thus the resulting electrical signal) would
remain the same during both moisture adsorption and desorption, as hydration and
dehydration occur symmetrically. However, as shown in Fig. 4a, the directions of
current signals during moisture adsorption and desorption are opposite, which aligns
well with our proposed mechanism: humidity fluctuations induce a concentration
gradient of mobile iodide ions, and this gradient drives their directional migration.
Based on the above analysis, we conclude that in our device, the hydration energy
of iodide ions is insufficient to dominate ion transport. Therefore, we focused our
discussion on the role of the humidity-induced ion concentration gradient.
We are grateful for your thoughtful suggestion, which has helped us to improve the
clarity and completeness of our explanation.

[Comment 4] While the proposed mechanism identifies PAMPS and NaI as the key
functional components in the SMEG system, the rationale for using P(AM-co-AMPS)
as the polymer matrix remains unclear. Although the authors note PAM's hydrophilic
nature, this alone does not sufficiently justify its incorporation into the copolymer
structure. Does PAM actively participate in power generation, or does it just play a role

advantages over pure PAMPS?
[Response] We sincerely thank you for this important question, which prompted us to
clarify the role of PAM in the system and to provide a more comprehensive rationale
for the copolymer design.
1. Role of PAM in the power generation process:
We agree that PAM does not directly participate in the moisture-driven power
generation mechanism. Instead, it mainly serves to provide structural support and
improve water retention. Experimental results from the PAM-NaI system show
negligible electrical output under humidity changes, confirming that PAM is not an
active functional component in the energy conversion process. Additionally, we
attempted to fabricate pure PAMPS hydrogels and found them to be highly brittle and
difficult to handle during preparation (see Supplementary Fig. 3 and Supplementary
Video-R). After soaking in the same NaI solution and exposure to ambient air for one
week, the pure PAMPS gels exhibited significant shrinkage, indicating limited water
retention, which may adversely affect ion mobility.
2. Advantages of P(AM-co-AMPS) over pure PAMPS:
The P(AM-co-AMPS) copolymer offers superior physical properties compared to
pure PAMPS. Pure PAMPS hydrogels are mechanically rigid and brittle, making them
susceptible to damage during swelling and deswelling cycles induced by humidity
fluctuations. This can compromise the structural integrity and long-term performance
of the device. Our performance tests also showed that PAMPS–NaI devices, although
initially outputting higher currents, suffered from rapid signal decay and poor cycling
stability (Fig. R4). In contrast, incorporating flexible AM segments into the copolymer
improves chain mobility and mechanical toughness, enabling the formation of a more
robust and elastic network. This enhances device durability and supports stable
operation over time.
We have refined the relevant descriptions in the revised manuscript. We greatly
appreciate your valuable suggestions, which have helped us strengthen the explanation
of our material design rationale.

[Comment 3] Explain in detail how moisture leads to the alternating changes in the I-

[Response] In view of your foregoing comment, we have provided a more detailed
explanation in the manuscript regarding how humidity fluctuations drive the periodic
variation of I- concentration. The specific mechanism is as follows:
Assuming that the device, initially equilibrated under a moderate humidity
condition (e.g., 60% RH), is transferred to a higher humidity environment (e.g., 75%
RH), the top surface of the hydrogel begins to adsorb moisture. This adsorption
promotes the dissociation of nearby I - into I- and I . The dissociation of I - establishes
3 2 3
a top-to-bottom I- concentration gradient within the hydrogel, driving the downward
migration of I- ions along with associated water molecules, thereby generating an ionic
current. After a certain period, the system reaches a new equilibrium under the higher
humidity.
Subsequently, when the device is exposed to a lower humidity condition (e.g., 43%
RH), the hydrogel begins to desorb moisture from its top surface. In this state, I- and I
2
tend to re-coordinate to form I -, leading to a decrease in I- concentration at the surface.
migration of I- ions and produces an ionic current in the opposite direction.
With cyclic fluctuations in environmental humidity, the reversible dissociation and
recombination of I - cause alternating I- concentration gradients, which continuously
3
drive the oscillatory migration of I- ions. This mechanism enables the SMEG device to
sustainably generate alternating current (AC) output, as illustrated in Supplementary
Fig. 1.

“The ubiquitous presence of water in the environment provides a natural reservoir
for green energy1. Generating electricity through the electric coupling between
functional materials and various forms of water—such as flow, waves, droplets,
moisture and evaporation—a new type of energy conversion effect has emerged, which
is defined as hydrovoltaic technology2,3,4. Compared with conventional photovoltaic
and wind power technologies, which rely on intermittent and variable sources such as
sunlight and wind under specific environmental conditions, hydrovoltaic technology
demonstrates significant potential due to the ubiquity of water resources in nature5.
Among hydrovoltaic technologies, moisture- and evaporation-driven generators have
attracted increasing attention for their virtues of ubiquity, spontaneity, and direct current
output6. Evaporation-based power generation represents a novel, passive means of
energy harvesting that leverages natural processes instead of mechanical motion7.
However, its long-term performance is constrained by the reliance on continuous access
to liquid water and is susceptible to climatic fluctuations8. Moisture-electric generators
(MEGs) are destined to exploiting omnipresent power sources due to the abundance,
accessibility, and all-weather availability of moisture in the ambient environment9, 10, 11,
12.
Nevertheless, most existing MEGs operate in a unidirectional migration process
of water and ions13,14,15. When the water and ions migration tend to equilibrate, the
MEGs will stop outputting electrical energy, reflecting a limited power generation
duration (minutes to hours)16,17,18. Although numerous strategies have been developed
to enhance or maintain water and ion concentration gradients—such as constructing
asymmetric or heterogeneous structures19,20, optimizing electrodes21,22, and engineering
functional materials23. The number of directionally migrating ions introduced into the
system is inherently limited, resulting in a restricted duration of power generation.
Without external energy input, it is therefore challenging to achieve long-term and
sustainable electricity generation.”

From this table, it can be concluded that in most current moisture-electric
generators, the primary mechanism is moisture-induced directional ion migration. In
some high-performance devices, redox reactions may also play a role. While the DC
generation mode based on directional ion migration offers the advantage of easy direct
utilization, it relies on a limited supply of mobile ions, which imposes a limit on its
operational lifetime and often results in rapid performance degradation.
In contrast, the AC generation mode can continuously re-establish ion
concentration gradients through external humidity fluctuations. Theoretically speaking,
this enables perpetual power generation with a significantly lower degradation rate.
Therefore, the working mode demonstrated in this study highlights a theoretical
advantage in the context of sustainable power generation.

476 remains constrained by its relatively low output power and the gradual volatilization of
477 iodine. Future efforts integrating temperature–humidity coupling strategies, optimizing
478 electrode and interfacial architectures, and exploiting less volatile coordination species
